title: Once-Hot AI Trade Leaves Korean Stocks Struggling for Buyers
source_used: Business Standard (carrying the Bloomberg article by Charlotte Yang, Winnie Hsu and Abhishek Vishnoi)
key_facts: South Korea's stock market, worth $4.3 trillion, is losing relevance with investors: turnover is down 70% from its late-May peak, foreigners are retreating at the fastest pace in Asia and local retail investors are pulling back.
The Kospi was the world's best-performing major equities benchmark in the first half but has since lost 22%, the worst in the second half, while Taiwanese and US AI-heavy peers set new highs.

Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the two memory-chip makers central to the AI supply chain, account for over half of the Kospi's weighting; investors now question how long the memory-chip boom will last.
Foreign funds pulled $131 billion from Korean stocks this year, the most among major Asian markets, according to exchange data compiled by Bloomberg.
Samsung's shares fell on Thursday despite a nearly nine-fold surge in quarterly operating profit; combined buybacks of 55 trillion won ($41 billion) by Samsung and SK Hynix are nearing completion.
Retail margin loans are about 33 trillion won, down from a 38.6 trillion won peak in June; brokerage account balances have fallen to about 100 trillion won from a record near 140 trillion won.

Taiwan's Taiex, up 70% this year, beat the Kospi by about 23 percentage points last quarter, the widest margin since the turn of the century; UBS Global Wealth Management prefers Taiwan for tactical AI exposure.
Bloomberg notes the Kospi is still among the best performers for 2026 overall and that some investors see buying opportunities after the declines.

why_it_matters_hint: A market that led the AI trade in the first half is now losing buyers because its fortunes rest on two memory-chip makers whose boom investors doubt.
